profile.summary: ProtGPT2 is a protein language model for designing new protein sequences. It reads amino acid sequence text and generates further sequence, either from a start token alone or continuing a fragment the user supplies. The developers report that the sequences it writes keep the amino acid composition and secondary structure content of natural proteins while sitting in parts of protein space that known proteins do not cover. The same model can score an existing sequence by perplexity, and ProteinGym lists it as a single-sequence baseline in its zero-shot substitution benchmark.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtGPT2 uses the GPT2 Transformer architecture. It is a decoder-only model with 36 layers and a model dimension of 1280. It was trained with a causal language modelling objective: predict the next token from the tokens before it. Sequences are split into tokens by a byte pair encoding vocabulary trained on Swiss-Prot, so one token is a short run of amino acids rather than a single residue, and the card gives an average of four amino acids per token. Pre-training used the raw UniRef50 sequences with the FASTA headers removed.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model description; paper: Methods, Vocabulary encoding

sections.title: What the developers use it for
sections.body: The card describes three uses. The first is generation with no further training: give the start token or a fragment and sample continuations. The second is fine-tuning on a user's own sequence set with the Hugging Face run_clm.py script, so that generated sequences follow that set. The third is ranking candidate sequences by perplexity. The developers report that perplexity values correlate with AlphaFold2 pLDDT, and advise sampling many sequences and keeping those with the lowest perplexity. They state that they have no threshold separating a good from a bad perplexity value.

profile.summary: ChemLLM-7B-Chat is a chat language model for chemistry. It is built from InternLM2-Base-7B by instruction tuning, first on a general question and answer corpus and then on a mixture of that corpus with 7 million chemistry question and answer pairs assembled from chemical databases. It answers chemistry questions in text and accepts molecule notations such as SMILES. It is in this database because the DeepProtein benchmark prompted it for protein properties without fine-tuning it, not because its developers designed it for proteins.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ChemLLM is a chat language model, not a protein model. It starts from InternLM2-Base-7B and is instruction tuned in two stages. The first stage uses Multi-Corpus, 1.7 million question and answer pairs collected from Hugging Face, to build general language ability. The second stage mixes ChemData, 7 million instruction tuning question and answer pairs built from chemical databases with a template method, with Multi-Corpus again, so that chemical knowledge is added without losing general ability. The released config is an InternLM2 causal language model with 32 layers, hidden size 4096 and 32 attention heads.

sections.title: What it is built for
sections.body: The developers describe ChemLLM as a model for chemistry and molecule science, able to hold a dialogue about chemical tasks. The card's recommended system prompt says the model accepts SMILES strings, prefers to answer with IUPAC names, writes reactions as SMARTS and also accepts SELFIES. Nothing in the model's own sources describes protein sequence tasks. Its appearance in this database comes from the DeepProtein benchmark, which prompted it for protein properties and reports that it was not fine-tuned for them.

steps.title: Load the model and ask one question
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
import torch

model_name_or_id = "AI4Chem/ChemLLM-7B-Chat"

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_name_or_id, torch_dtype=torch.float16, device_map="auto",trust_remote_code=True)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_name_or_id,trust_remote_code=True)

prompt = "What is Molecule of Ibuprofen?"

inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to("cuda")

generation_config = GenerationConfig(
    do_sample=True,
    top_k=1,
    temperature=0.9,
    max_new_tokens=500,
    repetition_penalty=1.5,
    pad_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id
)

outputs = model.generate(**inputs, generation_config=generation_config)
print(tokenizer.decode(outputs[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
PY

profile.summary: DeepProt-T5 is a set of protein property predictors made by the DeepProtein authors. They took Prot-T5-XL, an existing protein language model, and fine-tuned it separately on each task of their benchmark, so there is one checkpoint per task rather than a single general model. Each checkpoint takes a protein sequence and returns the prediction for its task, for example a stability value, a subcellular location or a per-residue epitope label. The authors report it as the strongest entry in their own benchmark on several tasks.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; Fine-tuned models; Deep Prot-T5

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DeepProt-T5 is not a new architecture. The DeepProtein authors took Prot-T5-XL, a 3B parameter protein language model from ProtTrans, and fine-tuned it separately on each of their benchmark datasets with the Hugging Face trainer. The difference from their other protein language model runs is that the upstream weights are updated during training rather than frozen, which they call dynamic rather than fixed embeddings. Each task therefore has its own checkpoint, and together they form the series the paper calls DeepProt-T5.

sections.title: Training setup the authors report
sections.body: For the DeepProt-T5 fine-tunes the paper gives a learning rate of 0.00002 for every model and a batch size of 10, chosen to avoid memory errors, against a default of 0.0001 and batch size 32 for the library's other sequence models. The maximum number of training epochs for all models is 100. The fine-tuning ran on two 24 GB NVIDIA RTX 3090 cards.

profile.summary: ProtT5 is a protein language model from the ProtTrans project. It reads one amino acid sequence and returns a vector for every residue, which can be averaged into a single vector for the whole protein. Those vectors are then used as the input to a smaller predictor, or the model is fine-tuned on a labelled task. The ProtTrans authors report that for per-residue prediction these embeddings beat methods that use evolutionary information, without any database search. The record here is the Prot-T5 line in the DeepProtein benchmark, which ran Prot-T5-XL-UniRef50.
profile.summary_source_locator: Model card: Model description and Intended uses; paper: Abstract; DeepProtein: section on protein language models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 is built on the t5-3b architecture: an encoder-decoder Transformer with 24 encoder layers, 24 decoder layers, model dimension 1024 and 32 attention heads in the released config. Unlike the original T5, which denoises spans, it was pre-trained with a BART-like masked language modelling objective that masks 15 per cent of the amino acids. The tokenizer is per-residue with a vocabulary of 21 symbols, the sequence is upper-cased, the rare residues U, Z, O and B are mapped to X, and training sequences were cut or padded to 512 tokens. Training started from the ProtT5-XL-BFD checkpoint rather than from scratch.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Model description, Training procedure, Pretraining; config.json

sections.title: What it is used for
sections.body: The developers offer the model for feature extraction or as a starting point for fine-tuning. They say fine-tuning can be more accurate than using it as a fixed feature extractor, and that for feature extraction the encoder-side embeddings should be used rather than the decoder's. All reported ProtT5-XL-U50 results in the paper come from encoder embeddings, measured in half precision, and the developers report no loss from half precision. The repository also ships a script that writes per-residue or per-protein embeddings for a FASTA file.
sections.source_locator: Model card: Intended uses and limitations; README: Quick Start, Important note on ProtT5-XL-UniRef50

sections.body: ProtT5 is one line in a larger ProtTrans family. The README lists ProtT5-XL-UniRef50, ProtT5-XL-BFD, ProtT5-XXL-UniRef50 and ProtT5-XXL-BFD, alongside ProtBert, ProtBert-BFD, ProtAlbert, ProtXLNet and two ProtElectra models, each with a Hugging Face and a Zenodo download. The paper gives 3B parameters for the XL size and 11B for the XXL size. For ProtT5-XL-UniRef50 the weights repository holds three checkpoint files at the revision read here: pytorch_model.bin, pytorch_model_600k.bin and pytorch_model_723k.bin, each about 11.3 GB, so a result should name both the revision and which file was loaded. The README also points at a half-precision encoder-only repository, Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc, which its quick start example loads instead.

run_guide.summary: Install the three packages the README names, then produce per-residue and per-protein ProtT5 embeddings for two short sequences.
prerequisites: Python with torch, transformers and sentencepiece, as the README installation section lists.
The README notes that a change in the T5 tokenizer can raise an error about sentencepiece_model_pb2, fixed by installing protobuf.
A GPU is optional. The README example falls back to CPU, and says half precision is GPU only and that CPU use is much slower.
Disk space for the checkpoint: each weights file in Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_uniref50 is about 11.3 GB, and the half-precision encoder repository used in the quick start is smaller.

steps.title: Install the packages
steps.shell:
pip install torch
pip install transformers
pip install sentencepiece
pip install protobuf
steps.explanation: The first three lines are the README installation block. The fourth is the fix the README gives for the T5 tokenizer error.

steps.title: Embed two sequences
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from transformers import T5Tokenizer, T5EncoderModel
import torch
import re

device = torch.device('cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
tokenizer = T5Tokenizer.from_pretrained('Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc', do_lower_case=False)
model = T5EncoderModel.from_pretrained("Rostlab/prot_t5_xl_half_uniref50-enc").to(device)
if device == torch.device("cpu"):
    model.to(torch.float32)
sequence_examples = ["PRTEINO", "SEQWENCE"]
sequence_examples = [" ".join(list(re.sub(r"[UZOB]", "X", sequence))) for sequence in sequence_examples]
ids = tokenizer(sequence_examples, add_special_tokens=True, padding="longest")
input_ids = torch.tensor(ids['input_ids']).to(device)
attention_mask = torch.tensor(ids['attention_mask']).to(device)
with torch.no_grad():
    embedding_repr = model(input_ids=input_ids, attention_mask=attention_mask)
emb_0 = embedding_repr.last_hidden_state[0,:7]
emb_0_per_protein = emb_0.mean(dim=0)
print(emb_0.shape, emb_0_per_protein.shape)
PY

profile.summary: ESCOTT predicts how damaging each possible amino acid substitution in a protein would be. It is not a trained network: it scores mutations from a multiple sequence alignment the user supplies, using the evolutionary distances between natural sequences to capture epistasis and conservation, together with a model structure such as one from AlphaFold. The output is a complete matrix of predicted effects for the protein. ESCOTT is one of two programs in the PRESCOTT package; the other, PRESCOTT, adjusts these scores with population allele frequencies from gnomAD for clinical classification.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ESCOTT scores a missense mutation from two sources of information. The first is evolutionary: the distances between natural sequences in a multiple sequence alignment, which carry both epistatic information and the conservation of each position, following the GEMME approach. The second is structural: a model structure, in practice from AlphaFold. The score combines an epistatic term and an independent term, with a linear coefficient set to 0.6 by default in favour of the epistatic term. Without a structure file the program still produces a full mutational matrix, which the paper says then corresponds to iGEMME, their improved version of GEMME. ESCOTT is the part of the PRESCOTT package that does not use allele frequencies; PRESCOTT then adjusts ESCOTT scores using gnomAD population frequencies.

sections.title: What it needs and what it gives back
sections.body: ESCOTT takes a multiple sequence alignment in FASTA format, with the query protein as the first sequence and no gaps in it, and optionally but preferably a structure in PDB format. By default it predicts the effect of every possible single substitution at every position; a mutations file can restrict that, and multiple substitutions can be combined on one line. The developers warn that an alignment from ColabFold may contain gaps in the query sequence that have to be removed first, and that each alignment needs enough sequences.

profile.summary: VESPA predicts the effect of single amino acid substitutions in a protein from the sequence alone, with no multiple sequence alignment and no structure. It embeds the sequence with the ProtT5 protein language model, predicts how conserved each residue is, extracts the language model's log-odds ratios for each substitution, and feeds all of that together with BLOSUM62 substitution scores into a logistic regression ensemble that outputs an effect score for every possible substitution. The authors report it as competitive with alignment-based predictors on deep mutational scanning data, although it was fitted without any such data.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: VESPA runs a pipeline of four steps. First it embeds the sequence with ProtT5. Second it predicts per-residue conservation in nine classes from that embedding, as defined by ConSurf-DB. Third it extracts per-variant log-odds ratios of masked marginal probabilities from ProtT5. Fourth it feeds the conservation prediction, BLOSUM62 substitution scores and those mask reconstruction probabilities into a balanced logistic regression ensemble, which outputs the effect score. The ensemble is ten logistic regressions trained on rotated cross-validation splits of Eff10k, a set of 100,737 binary variant effect annotations from 9,594 proteins, sharing one set of hyper-parameters. No deep mutational scanning data was used to fit it.

profile.summary: Evotuned UniRep is the UniRep protein representation model after extra unsupervised training on sequences related to the protein of interest, a step its developers call evotuning. The starting point is the pretrained 1900 unit multiplicative LSTM; the published evotuned checkpoint was made with 13,000 unsupervised weight updates on fluorescent protein homologues found with JackHMMER. The result is a representation, or a sequence likelihood, tuned to one protein family rather than to all of UniRef50. For a different family the evotuning has to be repeated with that family's sequences.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Evotuned UniRep is the UniRep multiplicative LSTM after further unsupervised training on sequences related to the target protein, a step the developers call evotuning. The released evotuned weights are a TensorFlow checkpoint taken after 13,000 unsupervised weight updates on fluorescent protein homologues found with JackHMMER, starting from the globally pretrained 1900 unit UniRep. A second checkpoint is released for the same procedure starting from random weights instead of the pretrained model, so the two can be compared. In ProteinGym the method is listed as single sequence with a multiple sequence alignment used for the evotuning step, and the second repository ProteinGym names gives a script that evotunes UniRep with an alignment file as input and another that computes log likelihoods from the evotuned model.

sections.title: Running it in practice
sections.body: The developers recommend their Docker environments, one for CPU and one for GPU, both built on a TensorFlow 1.3 image over Ubuntu 16.04, which launch a Jupyter notebook tutorial. The weight files are fetched from a public S3 bucket with the AWS command line tool and no credentials. The README warns that back propagation through an mLSTM of this size is memory hungry and that the main driver is the maximum input sequence length rather than the batch size: they fine tuned on fluorescent proteins of about 120 to 280 residues on a 16 GB GPU instance, and they note the full model needs more than 16 GB of RAM while the 64 unit model runs anywhere.

profile.summary: This is the autoregressive sequence model released as SeqDesign by Shin and colleagues, which ProteinGym lists as WaveNet. It learns the probability of a protein sequence residue by residue from a set of unaligned family sequences, using a dilated convolutional network rather than a recurrent one. Because it needs no alignment it can score insertions and deletions as well as single substitutions, by comparing the log probability of a mutant sequence with the wild type, and the same trained model can generate new sequences. There is no pretrained checkpoint: a model is trained for each protein family.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model learns the probability of a protein sequence one residue at a time, from unaligned sequences of a protein family. Instead of a recurrent network it uses a residual causal dilated convolutional network: six blocks of nine dilated convolutional layers, with weight normalisation and layer normalisation, dropout at 0.5 after each block and L2 regularisation on the weights. The authors say the number of blocks and layers was chosen to cover protein sequences of any length. To score a variant, the model gives the log probability of the mutant sequence; because no alignment is needed, insertions and deletions can be scored as well as substitutions.

sections.title: How a model is trained and used
sections.body: A model is fitted per protein family: the training input is a FASTA file of that family's sequences, with an optional weight appended to each header, and the README's single command trains it. Prediction then scores a FASTA of variants into a CSV. The README offers two prediction settings: deterministic, with dropout kept at 1.0 and one sample, or an average of 500 samples at dropout 0.5. The same trained model can also generate new sequences. In the paper, six models are built for each family, three replicates in each of the two reading directions, each trained for 250,000 updates with Adam, batch size 30 and channel size 48.

The paper's code availability note gives the repository and a Zenodo deposit. Because a model is trained per family, a reported result has to name the training sequence set, the branch or commit, the reading direction and replicate, and the prediction setting (deterministic or the 500 sample average).

profile.summary: PoET (Protein Evolutionary Transformer) is a generative protein language model that treats a whole protein family as one long sequence of related sequences. Given a set of homologous sequences for a protein of interest, it scores variants of that protein or generates new family members. The released code scores a list of variants against a multiple sequence alignment (MSA) of homologues and writes one fitness score per variant.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README: Scoring variants

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PoET is a stack of Tiered Transformer decoder layers with causal self-attention. Each layer works in two phases: it first attends within each sequence, then attends across the whole set of sequences joined together. Tokens are modelled in order within a sequence, while the order of sequences in the set does not matter. Training used 29 million sets of homologous sequences, one set per UniRef50 (version 2103) sequence with its UniRef50 homologues found by Diamond. To score variants, PoET conditions on homologues retrieved for the wild-type sequence (the final method uses the ColabFold protocol) and averages the conditional log-likelihoods over 15 subsamples of those homologues.

profile.summary: UniRep is a protein sequence representation model: a multiplicative LSTM trained on unlabelled sequences from UniRef50, which turns an amino acid sequence into a fixed length vector. Simple models fitted on that vector predict protein properties, and the same model can also generate sequences, which the developers call babbling. Three sizes are released with trained weights, 64, 256 and 1900 hidden units, together with the evotuned weights that come from further unsupervised training on one protein family.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UniRep is a multiplicative LSTM trained on unlabelled protein sequences, which the repository calls a babbler. Running a sequence through it gives a fixed length representation, and simple models fitted on that representation predict properties such as stability or mutant function. The repository provides three sizes, 64, 256 and 1900 hidden units, each with trained weights, and the same interface supports inferring representations, further training and generating sequences. The 1900 unit model is the full one. The custom model file in the repository holds the GRU, LSTM and mLSTM cell implementations used for the representation training on UniRef50.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Several weight sets are published on a public S3 bucket, each as its own directory: trained weights for the 1900, 256 and 64 unit models; the random initialisations that were used to begin evotuning, which the README says are provided to make that reproducible; the evotuned 1900 unit weights from the pretrained model; and the evotuned 1900 unit weights from a random start. A result should name which of these directories it used, and whether any further evotuning was done by the user, since the developers publish only the fluorescent protein evotuning.

sections.title: Running it in practice
sections.body: The developers recommend their Docker environments, one for CPU and one for GPU, both built on a TensorFlow 1.3 image over Ubuntu 16.04, which launch a Jupyter notebook tutorial. The weight files are fetched from a public S3 bucket with the AWS command line tool and no credentials. The README warns that back propagation through an mLSTM of this size is memory hungry and that the main driver is the maximum input sequence length rather than the batch size: they fine tuned on fluorescent proteins of about 120 to 280 residues on a 16 GB GPU instance, and they note the full model needs more than 16 GB of RAM while the 64 unit model runs anywhere.

profile.summary: Protein-RAG is a family of retrieval-augmented protein language models from GenBio AI, published under the names AIDO.Protein-RAG and AIDO.RAGPLM and now served as GB.Protein-RAG. Each model takes a protein sequence together with a retrieved multiple sequence alignment of homologues and, in the larger versions, per-residue structure embeddings, and it predicts masked residues. The embeddings and logits are used for contact prediction, structure prediction and fitness prediction. The models are released on Hugging Face and run through the ModelGenerator framework.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The models are transformer encoders trained with masked language modelling on a query sequence concatenated with its retrieved homologues. Two-dimensional rotary position embeddings let the model tell which chain a token belongs to and which residue index it holds. Masking is applied by column: when a residue of the query is selected, the aligned residues in every homologue are masked too, which stops the answer leaking from the alignment. The 16B models add structure: per-residue embeddings of dimension 384, produced by GenBio's structure tokenizer, are projected to the model width and added to the query token embeddings, and the loss is a weighted sum of a sequence term and a structure term. The 3B model uses dense MLP blocks; the 16B models replace them with sparse mixture-of-experts layers that route each token to two experts.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are published: GB.Protein-RAG-3B, GB.Protein-RAG-16B and GB.Protein-RAG-16B-proteingym-dms-zeroshot. The 3B model is the one the preprint names; it was fine-tuned from a 3-billion-parameter masked language model on 100 billion tokens of alignment data. The 16B model was built from GB.Protein-16B in three stages: position embedding fine-tuning on 10 billion tokens, 100 billion tokens of UniRef50 and UniClust30 alignments, then 80 billion tokens of AlphaFold Database alignments and structure tokens. The zero-shot checkpoint follows the same recipe but with 23 billion tokens in the third stage and a structure loss weight of 0.025 instead of 0.01. The models were first published under AIDO names; the old Hugging Face address for the 3B model now serves the repository named GB.Protein-RAG-3B, and the ModelGenerator backbone registry maps aido_protein_rag_16b and aido_protein_rag_3b to the gb_ names. A result should name the checkpoint, its revision and the backbone name used.

rep = model(src, nodes, edges, connections, edge_mask)

profile.summary: MULAN is a protein language model that reads a protein's sequence together with its three-dimensional structure, and returns per-residue or whole-protein embeddings. The structure enters as backbone and side-chain torsion angles, handled by a small added module called the Structure Adapter, whose output is added to the embeddings of a pretrained ESM-2 model that is then fine-tuned. The embeddings are meant to be used as features for downstream predictors.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MULAN keeps a pretrained ESM-2 encoder and adds a Structure Adapter: an MLP that turns each residue's torsion angles into an embedding, followed by one Transformer layer with rotary position embeddings. Each residue is described by the backbone angles phi and psi and up to five side-chain chi angles, with missing values filled by a reserved padding value. The angle embeddings are added to ESM-2's residue embeddings and the whole model is fine-tuned with the masked language modelling objective of ESM-2, masking 15% of tokens, and masking angles along with their residues. For AlphaFold2 structures, angles of residues with low confidence are masked.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three checkpoints are released on Hugging Face: MULAN-small, MULAN-ESM2-35M and MULAN-ESM2-650M. The Hugging Face listing for this author holds only these three models, so the SaProt-initialised variants the repository describes are not published there. steps.title: Extract embeddings for a folder of structures
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import numpy as np
import torch
from torch.utils.data import DataLoader

from mulan.dataset import ProteinDataset, data_collate_fn_dynamic
from mulan.model import StructEsmForMaskedLM
from mulan.model_utils import auto_detect_base_tokenizer

protein_data_path = './example_structures'
saved_dataset_path = './example_dataset'
is_experimental_structure = False
use_foldseek_sequences = False

dataset = ProteinDataset(
    protein_data_path=protein_data_path,
    saved_dataset_path=saved_dataset_path,
    use_foldseek_sequences=use_foldseek_sequences,
    is_experimental_structure=is_experimental_structure,
)

model = StructEsmForMaskedLM.from_pretrained(
    'DFrolova/MULAN-small',
    device_map="auto",
)
device = 'cuda:0' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
model.to(device)

esm_tokenizer = auto_detect_base_tokenizer(model.config, use_foldseek_sequences)

def data_collator(x):
    if use_foldseek_sequences:
        one_letter_aas = esm_tokenizer.all_tokens[5:]
    else:
        one_letter_aas = dataset.tokenizer.one_letter_aas

    return data_collate_fn_dynamic(x,
        esm_tokenizer=esm_tokenizer,
        nan_value=np.deg2rad(dataset.tokenizer.nan_fill_value),
        mask_inputs=False,
        all_amino_acids=one_letter_aas,
        use_foldseek_sequences=use_foldseek_sequences)

dataloader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=1, shuffle=False, collate_fn=data_collator)

with torch.no_grad():
    for i, (batch, batch_names) in enumerate(zip(dataloader, dataset.protein_names)):
        struct_inputs = [struct_input.to(device) for struct_input in batch['struct_inputs']]
        embeddings = model(
            input_ids=batch['input_ids'].to(device),
            attention_mask=batch['attention_mask'].to(device),
            struct_inputs=struct_inputs,
            output_hidden_states=True
        )['hidden_states'][-1]
        embeddings = embeddings[0][1:-1]
        protein_embedding = embeddings.mean(dim=0)
        print(batch_names, embeddings.shape, protein_embedding.shape)
PY

profile.summary: S2F (Sequence-Structure Fitness model) predicts how amino acid substitutions change protein fitness without training on any fitness data. profile.summary: SiteRM is a phylogenetic model, not a neural network. Given a multiple sequence alignment of a protein family, it fits a separate 21 by 21 amino acid substitution rate matrix for every column of the alignment, with the classical LG rate matrix as a prior. For variant effect prediction it scores a mutant by the log probability of mutating away from the wild-type residue at each site after one unit of evolutionary time, summed over sites. It is distributed inside the CherryML Python package, together with FastCherries, the fast tree estimator that makes the fitting practical.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and section 4; README: Introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: SiteRM extends the LG model of amino acid evolution by giving each alignment column its own rate matrix. Fitting runs in two steps: FastCherries estimates the cherries of the tree and the per-site rates from the alignment alone, then CherryML's optimiser estimates a rate matrix per site, regularised towards a prior matrix. The authors use the LG matrix as the prior with regularisation strength 0.5, so half the counts come from pseudocounts, and they treat the gap as a 21st state. A variant is scored as the sum over mutated sites of the log transition probability from the wild-type residue to the mutant residue at evolutionary time t = 1, which makes it an independent-sites model with additive per-site effects conditioned on the wild type.
sections.source_locator: Paper: sections 3.4 and 4; README: Introduction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are no weights: the model is fitted from the alignment each time it is used, so a result is defined by the alignments, the code version and the settings. The settings that matter are the prior rate matrix, the regularisation strength, the number of rate categories, the alphabet used for site rates against the alphabet used for the rate matrices, the evolutionary time, and the number of epochs. The ProteinGym scoring script fixes regularisation strength 0.5, evolutionary time 1.0, the lg.txt prior for tree estimation and lg_with_gaps.txt for regularisation, and device cpu. The package is on PyPI as cherryml, so a result should also name the package version or the commit used.
sections.source_locator: README: SiteRM/FastCherries Python API; ProteinGym scoring script

sections.title: Why an independent-sites model
sections.body: The authors argue that the gain over models that learn interactions between sites comes from conditioning on the wild-type residue, which the competing approaches do not do, and from being able to fit family and site specific matrices on very large alignments without overfitting. The largest alignment they processed had about 454,000 distinct sequences of length 364, which took FastCherries about 1,000 seconds on one CPU core, plus about one second per site for the rate matrices.

strengths.text: Runs on CPU and scales to very large alignments: the authors report about 1,000 seconds on one core for an alignment of roughly 454,000 sequences, and FastCherries is 10 to 100 times faster than FastTree.
The whole ProteinGym substitution benchmark is reported to take about two hours on eight CPU cores of a laptop.
The authors report an AUC of 0.911 on the human clinical benchmark and say SiteRM beats ESM1v and ESM-IF1 on Spearman, AUC, MCC and NDCG in their table; these are the authors' own claims.
No weights to manage: the model is fitted from the alignment, so there is nothing to version except the code and the settings.

limitations.text: An alignment is required for every protein, and the quality and depth of that alignment set the result.
Sites are modelled independently, so interactions between positions are not represented; the authors present this as a deliberate choice.
The method assumes time-reversible evolution and carries a small asymptotic bias, which the authors list as limitations.
Installation has system dependencies (compilers, Boost, GSL, MPI) and was tested on Ubuntu 20.04 with Python 3.10; third-party phylogenetics tools are built locally if missing.

run_guide.summary: Install the cherryml package and fit site-specific rate matrices for one alignment with the SiteRM training function.
prerequisites: Python 3.10 on Ubuntu 20.04 is the tested setup.
System packages listed in the README: autoconf, automake, gcc, libboost-dev, libboost-regex-dev, libgsl-dev, libopenmpi-dev, mpich, pkg-config, wget, zlib1g-dev, and open-mpi.
CPU is enough. The vectorised implementation can use a GPU with device="cuda"; the non-vectorised one is CPU only and uses less memory.
An alignment for the protein family, and a prior rate matrix such as the LG matrix shipped in the repository.

steps.title: Install the package
steps.shell: pip install cherryml
steps.explanation: The README's user install. A developer install from source is also described, with a conda environment on Python 3.10 and a cython build step.

steps.title: Get the repository for the prior matrices and the test alignment
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/songlab-cal/CherryML.git
cd CherryML
git checkout --detach 8ff221a468810f672a086ba6d27fd163d96159cc
steps.explanation: The commands below read rate matrices under data/rate_matrices/ and an alignment under tests/data/, and the README's own examples read alignments under demo_data/. These clone and checkout lines are added to get the repository at the commit this page was written from.

steps.title: Fit SiteRM on one protein alignment
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from cherryml import learn_site_specific_rate_matrices
from cherryml import io as cherryml_io
from cherryml.utils import get_amino_acids

msa = cherryml_io.read_msa("tests/data/Aln0037_txt-gb_phyml.txt")
res_dict = learn_site_specific_rate_matrices(
    tree=None,
    msa=msa,
    alphabet=get_amino_acids(),
    regularization_rate_matrix=cherryml_io.read_rate_matrix("data/rate_matrices/equ.txt"),
    regularization_strength=0.5,
    alphabet_for_site_rate_estimation=get_amino_acids(),
    rate_matrix_for_site_rate_estimation=cherryml_io.read_rate_matrix("data/rate_matrices/equ.txt"),
    num_epochs=30,
)
print(res_dict["learnt_rate_matrices"].shape)
print(len(res_dict["learnt_site_rates"]))
PY
steps.explanation: The repository's own test function test_learn_site_specific_rate_matrices_real_vectorized_GOAT_with_fast_cherries_proteins, wrapped in a shell heredoc and run from the repository root. Its os.path.join of the module directory is replaced by the alignment's path from the repository root, and the two print lines are added. tree=None lets FastCherries estimate the tree. For the paper's variant effect setting, use the LG prior at data/rate_matrices/lg.txt and lg_with_gaps.txt instead of equ.txt, as the ProteinGym script does.
steps.source_locator: cherryml/_siterm_public_api.py: test_learn_site_specific_rate_matrices_real_vectorized_GOAT_with_fast_cherries_proteins; README: Python API; ProteinGym script

steps.title: Or reproduce the ProteinGym substitution scores
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/OATML-Markslab/ProteinGym.git
cd ProteinGym
git checkout --detach 144fe22b07dfaeec2b366f2346203a9838a55b4c
cd scripts/scoring_DMS_zero_shot/
bash scoring_SiteRM_substitutions.sh
steps.explanation: This runs in the ProteinGym repository, not CherryML, so the clone and checkout lines pin it to the commit the script was read from. The CherryML README directs readers there, and the script installs cherryml itself, then calls proteingym.baselines.SiteRM.compute_fitness over the benchmark assays. The README says to follow it with merge_all_scores.sh and performance_substitutions.sh, and that num_processes can be set to the cores available.
steps.source_locator: README: ProteinGym results; ProteinGym scoring script

outputs: From the Python call: the shape of the array of per-site rate matrices and the number of learnt site rates. From the ProteinGym script: score files under the SiteRM output folder set by output_scores_folder.
limitations: These commands were read from the repository and the ProteinGym script and have not been executed by Rewire.
The Python step is a test function from inside the package, adapted to run from the repository root; it is not a documented public example.
pip install cherryml is not pinned to a version in the README, so the installed code may differ from the commit read here.
The clinical benchmark run is much longer: the README says around a full day because there are ten times more alignments.

uc20260930-model-siterm.notes: SiteRM has no weights: it is fitted on the user's alignment, so Parameters and Weights licence are marked inapplicable. It ships inside the CherryML package together with FastCherries and the earlier CherryML work, which are separate methods from the same group. The ProteinGym scoring script was fetched from the ProteinGym repository at the commit already attached to this record, because the CherryML README directs readers there for the benchmark run.
